newsitem.title: UK: UK buybacks in question after Barclays move.
newsitem.headline: UK buybacks in question after Barclays move.

text.p: A lukewarm market response to Barclays Plc's 300 million pound ($488 million) share buyback has raised questions over buybacks after the withdrawal last year of special tax loopholes, market experts said on Monday.

Barclays sent its brokers into the market last Wednesday with a target of purchasing up to 26 million shares, but succeeded in snapping up only 9.2 million -- giving a clear signal of the changing attitude of large shareholders.
Pundits said the failure showed that the conduct of buybacks would have to change, although as yet there was no single clear alternative.

"Tactics concerning buybacks will clearly have to be re-thought," said Philip Isherwood, stock market strategist at brokerage Dresdner Kleinwort Benson. "Companies have to deal with the fact that the environment they are operating in has changed."

Last October Bluebird Toys Plc was the last British company to operate a share repurchase before the Treasury rule changes. Bluebird said with its annual results on Monday that it planned to seek authorisation for further share buybacks this year.
But Bluebird's finance director David Sandilands told Reuters: "We will have to examine other options. Quite what the outcome may be remains to be seen."

Asked whether an alternative to a share buy back could be large special dividends, he said: "A large dividend is to the detriment of large individual (tax-paying) shareholders who might well be on the 40 percent tax rate."
"And the important point is that unlike a share repurchase scheme, it is not optional for shareholders."

Others pointed to recent initiatives by Yorkshire Water Plc and Southern Electric Plc -- involving the issue of special bonus or B shares to all shareholders -- as a possible way forward for some companies, particularly those like utilities with a large number of private shareholders.

Yorkshire's broker SBC Warburg said on Monday it would buy back its B shares at 36p, in line with a buyback plan announced in January. Southern said it had extended its offer to repurchase the shares following a strong response to the offer.

Ground rules for buybacks changed last October 8, when Chancellor Kenneth Clarke plugged tax loopholes to preempt a move by Reuters Holdings Plc to return some 613 million pounds to shareholders through an issue of special dividend shares and a consolidation of its ordinary shares.

The withdrawal of the loophole, which the Treasury said was expected to reap annual savings of some 400 million pounds, meant tax-exempt pension funds could no longer treat a buyback as a special dividend and then reclaim advance corporation tax which companies were deemed to have paid.
Reuters put its plans on ice and said recently it continued to assess the best way of returning surplus cash to shareholders.
Investment bankers said Barclays's experience showed that companies were still adapting to the fact that old-style buybacks were now much less likely to succeed.

"I think the big issue that this raises is that, whereas up to October 8 it was acceptable to go into the market and do a share buyback focused on specific institutional shareholders, now those institutions have to take an economic decision whether to sell," said one senior investment banker.

Companies were likely to have to pay a higher price than previously if they stuck to their old buyback practices -- risking the ire of smaller shareholders not able to participate directly in the offer, he said

Anyway, oldstyle buybacks were an unwieldy means of ridding a company of surplus cash. "I think what Barclays has shown is how clumsy it was...If a company buys back a chunk of stock it tends to effectively put a ceiling on its shares for some time," he said.

"Had Barclays been successful it would have shown there were sellers at that level, and you often see underperformance for months after a big buyback," the investment banker added. "And that is one of the reasons institutions don't like them."
